summary: Spinning Globe Jukebox uses NASA Earth Information Center visualization data to create sounds. When users spin a three dimensional model of the earth and use a needle to select any location on earth, the software will convert that location’s data into sound in real-time. Warmer waters have higher pitched tones and sharper fronts such as the Gulf Stream produce trembling tones when users select the ocean layers (ECCO2 sea surface temperature). Sea salt produces a whooshing sound, dust produces a hissing sound, smoke produces a crackling sound, and pollution produces a buzzing sound when users select the air layers (GEOS aerosol). Each frame of color was converted into value on a global grid. The Guided Tour feature along with screen-reader support and keyboard controls allow for blind and low vision individuals to access the Earth’s Story.
details:
Spinning Globe Jukebox creates sound from NASA's Earth Information Center visualizations so that users can "hear" the Earth as well as view it. Users rotate an interactive 3D globe and place a needle over any part of the Earth; then the Spinning Globe Jukebox app will play the data beneath that point in real-time. The globe is made up of two layers. One layer is called the ocean layer, and it utilizes NASA's ECCO2 sea surface temperature visualization. When the user rotates the globe and points the needle at a location, if there is warm water, then the app will produce a higher pitched sound. If there are sharp temperature differences, such as the Gulf Stream, then the app will produce a trembling sound. Cold polar waters will produce glassy pinging sounds. The other layer of the globe is referred to as the air layer. This layer utilizes NASA's GEOS global aerosols visualization. For example, sea salt produces a sound that resembles a surf whoosh. Dust produces a sound that resembles a sandy hiss and rumble. Smoke produces a sound that resembles a crackling fire. Sulfate pollution produces a sound that resembles a buzzing industrial drone. Users have the option to listen to either layer individually or simultaneously. In addition, users can determine if latitude will control the pitch register or the stereo position of the sounds. Users also have the option to take a guided tour of seven locations, each with its own caption. A small map displays the location of the needle on the original NASA visualization frame. In order to extract data from the visualizations, I used each pixel's color to find its corresponding value on the visualization frame's color scale. After finding the values, I averaged them across a 1-degree global grid. This provides sea temperature estimates within approximately ±1°C and aerosol strength estimates based on relative intensities for four types of particles. I verified that both visualization frames were aligned with actual coastal boundaries.

There are many advantages to this project. First, it will provide NASA's Earth observation data in audio format for people with visual impairments using screen readers, keyboard controls, and captioning. Second, it provides all people with another way to recognize trends that may go unnoticed when viewing maps (e.g., rapid changes in temperature, the boundaries of dust storms). Since it functions as one webpage without any software installation required, it can be used in classrooms, museum kiosks, or homes. Additionally, each audio file is linked to its corresponding NASA visualization, thus allowing users to view and listen to the same data at the same time. My goal is to make NASA's Earth observation science available to those individuals who cannot view a computer screen and to engage those individuals who do not relate well to graphical representations of data. Through enabling anyone to "hear" warm oceans, desert dust, and wildfire smoke, I intend to help make the processes occurring on Earth seem more tangible and memorable, thereby increasing comprehension of how Earth is evolving and encouraging more people to utilize NASA's open data.

I created the application using only HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. This is a single, self-contained website. To create the globe, I used the HTML Canvas 2D API to render the orthographic projection, which I wrote from scratch. To provide sound, I used the Web Audio API. I employed several different types of audio synthesis including oscillators, noise sources, filters, stereo panning, and a compressor. I processed the data for my application in Python using NumPy and Pillow. Finally, I tested the rendering capabilities of my application and its performance with Playwright and headless Chrome. During development, I relied upon Claude, an AI assistant, to assist me in writing the code and the text explaining the project. I worked on a laptop while listening to music through headphones.

I believe the creativity of my project is to make sonification something you can interact with. Many sonification projects have one time series played as a melody. In my project, you will move to a location, and then listen to what is happening at that location. This means the sound will vary depending upon your location. Each type of data has been assigned a sound that I felt was appropriate for the data. Temperature is represented by musical pitch, fronts are represented by a tremolo, and aerosols are represented by natural sounds (i.e., surf for sea salt, crackle for smoke) so that the user does not need to learn to recognize these sounds. Additionally, I used the data from NASA’s visual frames. Using the data from the visual frames allowed me to connect the visual with the audio components of the project directly. This was one of the requirements of the challenge.

I had multiple criteria when making decisions regarding the development of this application. From the very beginning of the process, I designed the application with accessibility in mind. To be honest with respect to scientific data, the application clearly identifies itself as using visual color scales and that the aerosol measurements are relative to each other rather than actual measurements. To make listening to the application enjoyable for users, I utilized a pentatonic scale to ensure that the notes do not clash. In addition, I created a smooth transition between different values. Finally, to avoid sudden volume increases, I employed a compressor. There were no flashing images in the application. The application will typically run at approximately 60 frames per second on most browsers. Users can easily learn how to use the application in less than a minute through a guided tour, live readouts, and a small map. I decided to develop a polished and fully functional two-layer demonstration instead of developing a larger and incomplete demonstration.
